contributions.headingText: Plasmacytoma is a solitary neoplasm of clonal plasma cells without evidence of plasma cell (multiple) myeloma or end-organ damage due to plasma cell neoplasia.

9731/3 Solitary plasmacytoma of bone

9734/3 Extramedullary plasmacytoma

SPB mainly arises in bones with active haematopoiesis, affecting the axial skeleton more often than the appendicular skeleton. The spine is most commonly involved, followed by pelvis, ribs, skull, and long bones {22549792; 22752147; 33145987; 33201300}.

EMP most commonly arises in the upper respiratory tract (nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, nasopharynx, larynx) {10357398; 15586381; 32934063; 33201300}. EMP rarely involves the lymph nodes {10357398; 11190797; 15586381}, lungs, gastrointestinal tract {10357398; 28056880}, genitourinary tract {10357398; 15586381}, and skin {10357398; 23000906}.

Patients present with localized pain, swelling, fracture, and/or spinal cord compression {22752147}. Approximately half of patients have a serum paraprotein; IgG is most common, followed by IgA, and rarely light chain only {22752147; 31707123; 32934063}. Rare patients with plasmacytoma have a paraneoplastic syndrome, such as POEMS syndrome (polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, myeloma protein, and skin changes) {22231043; 34000085}, TEMPI syndrome (telangiectases, elevated erythropoietin and erythrocytosis, monoclonal gammopathy, perinephric fluid collection, and intrapulmonary shunting), or AESOP syndrome (adenopathy and extensive skin patch overlying plasmacytoma) {32861309}.

Radiographically, SPB is a solitary lytic bone lesion {14608572; 16304406; 22549792; 30218303}.

The incidence rates of SPB and EMP in the USA are 0.45 cases per 100 000 person-years and 0.09 cases per 100 000 person-years, respectively {33270992}. About 2–5% of all plasma cell neoplasms are plasmacytomas {6668499; 12057071; 33145987}. EMP is less common than SPB {10580871}, accounting for 20–30% of all plasmacytomas {32934063; 33201300; 33270992}.

Plasmacytomas affect more men than women (M:F ratio: ~1.5–2:1 for SPB, ~2–3:1 for EMP) {28056880; 28393375; 31707123; 33270992}. Black people are at higher risk than White people for SPB, whereas Hispanic individuals have an intermediate risk {22654647; 33270992}. Risk for EMP shows less difference among racial groups {33270992}. Patients are mostly middle-aged and older adults (median age: 55–65 years) {16304406; 22549792; 22654647; 28056880}. Incidence increases with age {33270992}. Young adults are occasionally affected {16677383; 22549792; 33270992}.

EMP mainly arises in sites of ongoing antigen exposure. Rare posttransplantation plasmacytomas are related to immune dysregulation (see section Hyperplasias arising in immune deficiency/dysregulation).
Cytogenetic abnormalities in EMP overlap with those of plasma cell myeloma / multiple myeloma (see section Plasma cell myeloma / multiple myeloma) {18326524; 23000906}.
SPB is a soft, gelatinous, haemorrhagic lesion.

Neoplastic plasma cells grow in sheets. In bone, these cells replace marrow and trabeculae, sometimes causing fracture. The cellular morphology varies among cases. Some are composed of normal-appearing plasma cells; others of enlarged, atypical plasma cells with distinct nucleoli; and a few of plasmablasts with large nuclei, vesicular chromatin, and prominent central nucleoli {10357398; 11190797; 22231043}. Rare cases have anaplastic morphology {29388036} or amyloid deposition {25842207}. Dutcher bodies may be seen.

Immunophenotype

The immunophenotype is similar to that of plasma cell myeloma / multiple myeloma, except that expression of cyclin D1 and CD56 is rare or absent in EMP {15586381}. IgG is most commonly expressed, followed by IgA {10357398}. IgA+ EMP may have distinctive features, including frequent nodal as well as extranodal involvement, and a tendency to affect younger patients, some with immune dysregulation {20871216}. Plasmacytomas are almost always negative for EBV. Rare cases of EBV+ EMP in immunocompetent patients (EPIC) have been reported {25556356}. EPIC involves the nasal cavity and, less often, other head and neck sites or the gastrointestinal tract {9428372; 21442194; 22969303}. The histological and immunophenotypic features are similar to those of other EMPs, except that EPIC often contains many CD8+ T cells {25556356}. Rare EBV+ osseous plasmacytomas have been described {7894217; 25556356}.

Differential diagnosis

The presence of B cells and/or IgM expression suggests B-cell lymphoma with marked plasmacytic differentiation.

Plasmablastic morphology, tingible-body macrophages, a high proliferation index, and MYC rearrangements in an immunosuppressed or older patient, particularly in the oral cavity, suggest plasmablastic lymphoma. Plasmablastic lymphoma is usually EBV+, in contrast to the vast majority of plasmacytomas. Plasmacytoma can mimic a neuroendocrine neoplasm on routinely stained sections, and CD138 stains epithelial cells as well as plasma cells. A panel of immunostains including keratins, neuroendocrine markers, IRF4 (MUM1), and kappa and lambda can help establish a diagnosis.
On cytological preparations, SPB can show a spectrum of differentiation, from small bland plasma cells to plasma cells with atypia. Cases of EMP tend to be more differentiated.
Clonal IG gene rearrangement may assist in cases with ambiguous clonality by light chain immunohistochemistry, in situ hybridization, or flow cytometry.

Essential: a biopsy-proven clonal plasma cell neoplasm of bone or an extramedullary site; no clonal B cells; no other (plasma cell) lesions on physical examination or radiographic studies; no end-organ damage (hypercalcaemia, renal insufficiency, anaemia, and bone lesions [CRAB]) due to plasma cell neoplasm; < 10% clonal plasma cells on non-targeted bone marrow sampling – plasmacytomas with no marrow involvement must be distinguished from those with minimal (< 10%) marrow involvement.

Patients should undergo thorough evaluation to exclude plasma cell myeloma / multiple myeloma, including complete blood count; serum creatinine, calcium, and free light chains; serum and urine protein electrophoresis and immunofixation; bone marrow aspiration and biopsy to investigate the presence of clonal plasma cells (including flow cytometry, FISH, and conventional cytogenetics); and highly sensitive imaging with whole-body CT, PET-CT, or MRI.

Standard management of EMP comprises involved field radiation therapy, typically at doses of 40–45 Gy {29976492}. Local recurrences occur in 5–20% of cases {16229966; 18543343; 21437886}. The risk of progression of EMP to plasma cell myeloma is lower than that for SPB, with 5-year progression-free survival rates of 70–93% and 38–44%, respectively {21437886; 27605358}. Cytogenetic abnormalities in EMP appear to lack the prognostic significance they have in plasma cell myeloma / multiple myeloma (PCM/MM) {18326524; 23000906}.

Radiation is also standard therapy for SPB, providing effective local control in most cases. Without radiation-based treatment, the local recurrence rate is high {16677383; 22654647; 22752147; 34190199}. SPB > 50 mm is associated with an increased risk of local recurrence {16304406; 32739971; 32934063}. The risk of progression to PCM/MM increases with lesions > 50 mm {32739971}, older patient age, and persistent paraprotein > 1 year after therapy {16304406; 16677383; 22654647; 32934063}. Surgical resection helps stabilize affected vertebra and may decrease the risk of progression {31715413; 33145987}. Addition of systemic therapy may improve outcome {31707123}. Patients with SPB with minimal bone marrow involvement are significantly more likely to develop PCM/MM than those with no clonal plasma cells on bone marrow aspirate by flow cytometry or on biopsy by immunohistochemistry {22549792; 22654647; 24876564; 24939658; 25439696}; administering systemic, multiple myeloma–type therapy to such patients has been suggested {33549387}. Patients diagnosed more recently have a better prognosis, probably due to improved staging techniques and therapy {33145987; 33270992}. Plasmablastic morphology is associated with aggressive behaviour {25842207}. A subset of patients with SPB have a long survival (> 10 years) without progression to PCM/MM {22654647}.
